meta.what_this_is: One row per panel review finding, joining what the reviewer said, what the fix agent did with it, and an independent blind model adjudication of whether it is a real defect.
meta.how_the_labels_were_made: A fresh model session was shown the finding's file, line, lens, claim and prose — built by allowlist, with the panel's severity, the verifier's verdict, the gate outcome and the lane never read — plus the unified diff at that finding's own round and the repository files the finding cites. It answered is_real / severity / confidence / reasoning.
caveats: POPULATION IS BLOCKING-ONLY BY CONSTRUCTION. The channel these findings come from carries only severity critical|major AND lane != backlog, so every row is a finding that GATED a pull request. Minor and nit findings exist upstream and never reach this data.

NOT A SIMPLE RANDOM SAMPLE. Every finding the fix agent did not record as `fixed` entered with probability 1 (a certainty stratum); the rest were stratified by state x severity x lens, seed 20260820. Quote it as stratified-with-a-certainty-stratum.

MIXED INSTRUMENT. 84 labels were written by claude-fable-5 and 16 by claude-opus-5 (pr-786, pr-695) after a monthly quota was exhausted mid-run. The split is confounded with item identity. See label.annotators on each row.

SEVERITY IS THE RESULT. precision answers 'is it a real defect'; blocking_precision answers 'would an independent reader also block a merge on it'. They differ by a factor of ~4.5 and both belong in any quote.

FIX-AGENT PROSE IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT. A fix-agent note quotes the panel's severity and verdict back at itself, so a dataset carrying it could not be fed to an adjudicator without breaking the blinding this measurement depends on. Only the structured fields and the note LENGTH are here.

K=1, one replicate, so no inter-annotator agreement figure. Relative recall is not computable: the CodeRabbit arm produced 0 findings on all 19 agent-authored PRs. Absolute recall and the miss profile are permanently unmeasurable from a corpus assembled out of what reviewers found.

field_glossary.finding_key: stable identity: `<file>::<summary>`. The join key across every source.
field_glossary.panel.severity_stated: the reviewer's own severity word, after the workflow coerced unknown values to `major`
field_glossary.panel.gating / gating_basis: always unknown / lane-absent — the lane field does not survive the channel this data came from
field_glossary.fixer.disposition: fixed | skipped | disputed | unmatched — what the fix agent did. NOT a validity judgement (see caveats)
field_glossary.fixer.round_claim_* vs answering_claim_*: the claim on this finding's own round, vs the claim in the report that answered that round; they differ when a later fix round supersedes an earlier one
field_glossary.fixer.any_claim_status / any_claim_head: whether ANY report across all rounds claimed this finding, and the round head it was claimed at
field_glossary.fixer.matched_by_production_matcher: false means the shipped matchRebuttal would NOT have found this dispute — the tie-refusal defect, visible per row
field_glossary.fixer.note_chars: the LENGTH of the fix agent's note. The note text itself is deliberately not carried (see caveats)
field_glossary.adjudications: one entry per pass. `pass1` saw the diff only; `pass2`/`pass2b` also saw the cited files. Later passes are better evidenced.
field_glossary.label.*: the label of record, written from the last pass to judge that finding
field_glossary.label.presented_fields / withheld_fields: exactly what the adjudicator could and could not see — the blinding disclosure

panel.summary: Slides text-body style validation is stricter than the slides reader, so a GET → edit → PUT round-trip of an existing deck can now 400
panel.evidence: `assertValidTextBodyBlocks` calls `assertValidBlockStyle` (line 602), which throws on any present style value that is not a finite number (`value !== undefined && (typeof value !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(value))`, controller line 329-336) — so `lineHeight: null`, `marginTop: null`, or an alignment outside `BLOCK_ALIGNMENTS` is a 400. Unlike the docs arm, slide text bodies are persisted and returned VERBATIM (`writeSlidesRoot`/`readSlidesRoot` store plain JSON; the comment at line 570-576 states this explicitly and deliberately relaxes only the *structural* checks). Consequently a deck already holding such a value is readable through GET but no longer writable through PUT — the CLI read-modify-write flow breaks on data the caller never touched. The docs arm avoids this because `parseBlockStyleAttrs` drops the same values on read; the slides arm has no such normalizer. Either normalize on the slides read path or make the slides style check drop-and-continue instead of throwing.

findings.finding_key: packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts::anyone can start a `mode=cli` login pointing at an arbitrary loopback port; the new browser-binding cookie does not stop the start-url variant of the phishing attack it is documented as closing

panel.summary: Anyone can start a `mode=cli` login pointing at an arbitrary loopback port; the new browser-binding cookie does not stop the start-URL variant of the phishing attack it is documented as closing
panel.evidence: `GET /auth/github` is unauthenticated and accepts `mode=cli&port=<any 1024-65535>&nonce=<attacker's>&code_challenge=<attacker's>` from any origin (github-auth.guard.ts:98-129). The browser-binding cookie only rules out an attacker *pre-minting* a state in their own browser and replaying the callback; it does nothing when the attacker simply gets the victim to click the crafted **start** URL — the victim's own browser then mints the cookie, passes `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:190-200), and the server redirects the victim to `http://127.0.0.1:<attacker-chosen port>/callback?code=<victim's code>&state=<attacker's nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:145). Because the attacker chose the `code_challenge`, they hold the verifier, so PKCE does not protect the code either: an attacker with any listener on the victim's loopback (shared/multi-user host, or a malicious local helper) redeems the victim's code at `/auth/cli/exchange` and receives the victim's access + refresh tokens. The guard comment (github-auth.guard.ts:76-81) and the risk row in docs/design/rest-api.md:399 both assert the cookie closes 'an attacker mints a CLI state pointing at a loopback port they own and walks the victim through consent', which is only true for the callback-replay variant — a control that reads as covered but is not.

The code is minted for the victim's user (createCode(user.id,...)) and redirected to the attacker-chosen loopback port; since the attacker chose the challenge they hold the verifier, so PKCE and the nonce give no protection, and an attacker listener on a shared host redeems the victim's tokens. The cookie only defeats the attacker-pre-minted-state/callback-replay variant, so the guard comment and rest-api.md risk row overstate the protection — the claim is correct. findings.finding_key: packages/backend/src/auth/auth.controller.ts::cli auth code is still not bound to the client (no pkce); the nonce only gates the local listener, so an intercepted code is fully redeemable

panel.summary: CLI auth code is still not bound to the client (no PKCE); the nonce only gates the local listener, so an intercepted code is fully redeemable
panel.evidence: The change cites RFC 8252 §8.9, whose actual prescription for the loopback-redirect code-injection problem is PKCE. What landed is a `state` echo checked only inside the CLI's own listener (`packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:206`). The code itself remains an unbound bearer: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) takes `{ code }` with no authentication, no `code_verifier`, and no reference to the nonce — `consumeCode` looks up only the code (cli-auth.store.ts:71). Attack: anyone who observes the code within its 60s TTL — from the victim's browser history/URL bar (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…` is a real navigation), a browser extension, a shared/kiosk machine, or an intercepting proxy — POSTs it to /auth/cli/exchange and receives the victim's `accessToken` + `refreshToken`. The nonce does nothing here because the CLI listener is not in the path. Grepped the whole repo for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge: zero hits. Severity is 'major' rather than 'critical' because it needs code interception, and confidence is low because I could not demonstrate a concrete interception channel in this codebase.

fixer.note_prose: NOT CARRIED — see meta.caveats; a fix-agent note quotes the panel's verdict

pass1.reasoning: The diff confirms the claim: `cli-auth.store.ts` `createCode(userId)` stores nothing binding the code to the CLI instance, the nonce is only checked in the CLI's loopback listener (`login.ts` `nonceMatches`), and `docs/design/rest-api.md` in this PR documents `POST /auth/cli/exchange` as accepting `{ code }` with "no authentication required" and no verifier. An intercepted code is therefore fully redeemable by anyone — PKCE-style binding is absent. Impact is tempered by the 60s TTL, single-use semantics, and immediate redemption by the CLI, which confine exploitation to near-real-time interception, so I rate it minor rather than major; the description of the code as written is nonetheless correct. Confidence is medium because no checkout was mounted and I could not read the exchange handler itself, only the store and the PR's own documentation.

pass2.reasoning: Verified against the supplied sources: auth.controller.ts cliExchange (lines ~152-168) redeems `{ code }` with no authentication and no verifier, and cli-auth.store.ts `consumeCode` looks up only the code — the nonce is stored on the StateEntry, never the CodeEntry, and is checked only by the CLI's local listener (login.ts nonceMatches). So the code is an unbound bearer credential and an intercepted code within its 60s single-use TTL is fully redeemable, exactly as claimed; no PKCE exists anywhere in the change despite it citing RFC 8252 §8.9, whose prescription for loopback flows is PKCE. Severity is tempered by the 32-byte random, single-use, 60s code and the need for an interception channel (browser history after a timed-out flow, extension, local proxy), making this a defense-in-depth gap rather than a directly exploitable hole.

findings.finding_key: packages/backend/src/auth/oauth-state.ts::browser oauth `state` is an unauthenticated double-submit cookie with no `__host-` prefix and no server-side binding, so a sibling-subdomain foothold restores login csrf

panel.summary: Browser OAuth `state` is an unauthenticated double-submit cookie with no `__Host-` prefix and no server-side binding, so a sibling-subdomain foothold restores login CSRF
panel.evidence: `oauthStateCookieOptions()` sets `wafflebase_oauth_state` with `path:'/auth'` and no `__Host-` prefix (oauth-state.ts:57-68), and `webOAuthStateMatches` accepts any `state` whose SHA-256 preimage happens to be in that cookie (oauth-state.ts:47-55). The value is a bare random secret, not an HMAC over anything the server can re-derive. Cookie tossing is therefore the whole attack: an attacker who controls or XSSes ANY sibling host under the registrable domain (e.g. `blog.example.com`, a staging host, a takeover-able CNAME) sets `Set-Cookie: wafflebase_oauth_state=<their secret>; Domain=example.com; Path=/auth`, then navigates the victim to `/auth/github/callback?code=<code minted for the ATTACKER's GitHub account>&state=web.<sha256(their secret)>`. auth.controller.ts:148-159 finds a match, falls through to line 189-192, and issues `wafflebase_session`/`wafflebase_refresh` for the attacker's account in the victim's browser — the exact session-fixation the change set out to close. `__Host-` prefixing (which forbids `Domain=` and forces `Path=/`), or making `state` an HMAC over a server secret, removes the cookie-tossing degree of freedom. The same applies to `wafflebase_cli_confirm` (cli-login-confirm.middleware.ts:33-41), whose secret is likewise only proven by cookie possession.

The chain is coherent and the proposed __Host-/HMAC fixes are the correct mitigations. Caveat and reason for medium/major rather than high/critical: the attack requires attacker control of a sibling subdomain, and I cannot verify that the callback lacks any additional binding that would break the chain.

findings.finding_key: packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts::the cli login url — which carries the whole nonce + pkce challenge pair — is handed to `open()`, i.e. placed in a child process's argv, where any local user can read it and defeat all three new loopback bindings

panel.summary: The CLI login URL — which carries the whole nonce + PKCE challenge pair — is handed to `open()`, i.e. placed in a child process's argv, where any local user can read it and defeat all three new loopback bindings
panel.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` (login.ts:199) goes to great lengths to keep the authorization URL off stderr because "anyone who reads it can start their own login against the same pair and push the resulting code at this port", and writes it 0600 when stderr is not a TTY. But `openBrowser` (login.ts:176-184) passes the same URL to `open(url)`, which spawns `xdg-open <url>` / `open <url>` / a powershell shim with the URL as a command-line argument. On Linux with the default `hidepid=0` /proc (and on macOS via `ps`), any other local user sees `mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>&code_challenge=<challenge>` in full. Attack: local attacker reads the URL from `ps`; opens `https://server/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim's port>&nonce=<victim's nonce>&code_challenge=<victim's challenge>` in their own browser and consents as themselves; the backend mints a code bound to the copied challenge and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<victim port>/callback?code=A&state=<victim nonce>` — the same loopback the victim's CLI is listening on. The CLI's `nonceMatches` (login.ts:331) passes because the nonce was copied, and `POST /auth/cli/exchange` succeeds because the victim's verifier hashes to the copied challenge (cli-auth.store.ts:136). The victim's terminal is now logged into the attacker's account and every subsequent `wafflebase` write lands in the attacker's workspace — exactly the RFC 8252 §8.9 injection this change claims to close, on the multi-user host the change's own docs put in scope (docs/design/cli.md 'Browser binding').

I traced the exploit: because the authorization URL contains no backend state token, an attacker copies nonce+challenge+port, starts their own flow (satisfying the browser-binding cookie in their own browser), and the backend redirects a code bound to the attacker's account (carrying the copied challenge) to 127.0.0.1:<victim port>; on a shared host the victim's CLI accepts it (nonce matches) and the exchange succeeds since the copied challenge = S256(victim verifier), defeating all three bindings — the RFC 8252 §8.9 injection the change scopes multi-user hosts for. findings.finding_key: packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts::the cli oauth loopback callback has no `state`/csrf binding, so any local process or visited web page can inject an attacker's authorization code and silently log the cli into the attacker's account (pre-existing, out of diff)

panel.summary: The CLI OAuth loopback callback has no `state`/CSRF binding, so any local process or visited web page can inject an attacker's authorization code and silently log the CLI into the attacker's account (pre-existing, out of diff)
panel.evidence: `startCallbackServer` (login.ts:168-182) resolves on the first `GET /callback?code=<anything>` it receives from 127.0.0.1, with no `state` parameter generated, no `state` echoed in the OAuth URL built at line 36 (`?mode=cli&port=${port}`), no Origin/Sec-Fetch check, and no binding between the code and this CLI invocation. The code is then exchanged at line 56 and the resulting tokens persisted with `saveSession` (line 138). Vector: while `wafflebase login` is waiting (30s window, line 237), a page the user is browsing — or any unprivileged local process — issues `fetch`/`img src` to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker's code>` for candidate ports; the CLI exchanges the attacker's code and writes the attacker's `accessToken`/`refreshToken` and `activeWorkspace` into `~/.wafflebase/session.json`. Every subsequent `docs import` / `files upload` then writes the victim's data into the attacker's workspace. This is classic OAuth login-CSRF / session fixation. Out of the diff, but in the CLI auth path the diff's design doc explicitly discusses (`docs/design/cli.md`: 'The one command the flag does not hold back is `login`'). Fix: generate a random `state`, pass it in the OAuth URL, and reject a callback whose `state` does not match.

panel.summary: Image-fetch SSRF guard is check-then-connect: an attacker who controls DNS for a hostname they place in a document's image `src` can rebind between `assertResolvedHostIsPublic` and `fetch`, reaching 169.254.169.254 from the operator's machine.

The code comment at image-fetcher.ts:232-235 and docs/design/cli.md acknowledge this, but packages/cli/README.md:39 states without qualification that "A hostname is resolved before it is fetched and refused the same way if it answers with a non-public address" — a guard that reads as covering a named attack is the case nobody re-audits. panel.evidence: `isEmptyStoredColor` (packages/docs/src/model/color.ts:59-63) does `if (c === undefined) return false;` then `typeof c === 'string' ? ... : c.kind === 'srgb' && c.value.trim() === ''`. For `c === null` (typeof 'object', not undefined) it evaluates `c.kind` → `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null`. For `{ kind: 'srgb', value: 42 }` it evaluates `(42).trim()` → `TypeError: c.value.trim is not a function`. Before this delta the same input was harmless: `resolve(c === '' ? undefined : c)` passed `null` straight to the resolver, and slides' `makeColorResolver` (packages/slides/src/view/canvas/text-renderer.ts:55) returns the theme text color for `c == null`, while `resolveColor` (packages/slides/src/model/theme.ts:102) returns a non-string `value` verbatim without throwing. panel.evidence: The delta added a repair for `type === 'text'` before the generic `if (!data || typeof data !== 'object') return;` at packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts:640, but a `group` element still falls into that early return, and line 671 (`Array.isArray(data.children) ? data.children : []`) silently skips a non-array `children`. Consumers dereference it unconditionally: packages/slides/src/export/pdf.ts:227 `if (el.type === 'group') walk(el.data.children);`, packages/slides/src/model/group.ts:382 `result.push(...flattenElements(el.data.children));`, packages/slides/src/model/slide-size.ts:36 `if (el.type === 'group' && el.data.refSize == null)`. `migrateElement` (packages/slides/src/model/migrate.ts:155-156) returns non-shape elements untouched, so nothing repairs it on read — exactly the failure mode the new text repair exists to prevent, left reachable for groups.

The new tests and rest-api.md enumerate repairs for text data, table cell body, blocks/style/inlines — group data is not covered, and the PR's own docs state slides shapes are stored verbatim with migrateElement repairing shapes only, so nothing fixes it on read. I could not open pdf.ts:227/group.ts:382 to confirm the exact consumer dereferences (no checkout mounted), which is why confidence is medium, but the validator hole itself is unambiguous in the diff and matches the failure mode the PR fixed for the sibling element types.

findings.finding_key: packages/slides/src/export/pptx/color.ts::pptx color modifier attributes (`alpha`, `tint`, `shade`, `lummod`, `lumoff`) are still interpolated raw after this change removed the file's only xml escaping

panel.summary: PPTX color modifier attributes (`alpha`, `tint`, `shade`, `lumMod`, `lumOff`) are still interpolated raw after this change removed the file's only XML escaping
panel.evidence:
This diff deletes `import { escapeXmlAttr } from './xml.js'` from `color.ts` and replaces the escaped hex with `toRgbHexColor(c.value) ?? '000000'`, on the stated theory that normalization subsumes escaping. But lines 25-29 of the same function still do `mods.push(`<a:lumMod val="${c.lumMod}"/>`)` … `<a:alpha val="${c.alpha}"/>` with no coercion, and after this change nothing in the file escapes anything.

Vector: those fields are typed `number` but are *persisted JSON*. `packages/backend/src/yorkie/slides-tree.ts:101-104` assigns `root.slides = document.slides` verbatim, and `assertValidElement` (packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts:393-413) validates only `id`, `type` and `frame` — element `fill`/`stroke`/`effects` colors are never inspected. An authenticated workspace member (or an API key) PUTs an element whose fill is `{ kind: 'srgb', value: '#ffffff', alpha: '0"/><a:hlinkClick r:id="rId2' }`. When any user later exports the deck, `fillXml → solidFillXml → colorChildXml` emits `<a:alpha val="0"/><a:hlinkClick r:id="rId2"/>` — attacker-chosen OOXML elements inside the generated slide part.

The same sink is reachable from the function this diff actually rewrote: `packages/slides/src/export/pptx/text.ts:213-216` copies `out.tint = c.tint; out.shade = c.shade` straight off an untrusted docs `StoredColor` role object, so `{ kind:'role', role:'accent1', tint:'1"/><a:alpha val="0' }` on an inline style reaches `<a:tint val=…>` unescaped even though the srgb arm right above it is now normalized.

pass1.reasoning: The diff for packages/slides/src/export/pptx/color.ts deletes the file's only escaping import (escapeXmlAttr) and normalizes only the srgbClr/schemeClr `val`, while `${inner}` — built from the alpha/tint/shade/lumMod modifier children the PR's own slides-pptx-export.md documents ("alpha → child <a:alpha val>") — is still interpolated with no visible coercion. The PR itself establishes that such typed-but-persisted numbers are untrusted at these sinks (it added listLevelAttr in text.ts for the identical reason, and the lessons file says static types are "a claim, not a guarantee"), and storedColorToThemeColor's role arm visibly carries the untrusted object through to colorChildXml. I could not read the actual modifier-push lines (25–29) or assertValidElement since no checkout is mounted, hence medium confidence, but everything visible in the diff corroborates the claim and nothing contradicts it: the modifier attributes remain a raw interpolation sink after the change removed all escaping from the file.

pass2.reasoning: Verified in packages/slides/src/export/pptx/color.ts: colorChildXml interpolates lumMod/lumOff/tint/shade/alpha into XML attributes with no coercion or escaping, and the diff removed the file's only escapeXmlAttr use. Verified in packages/slides/src/export/pptx/text.ts that storedColorToThemeColor copies tint/shade verbatim from persisted StoredColor role objects into that sink, so the untrusted-string chain the claim describes exists; the PR's own threat model (Map lookups, listLevel clamping, "the static type is a claim") treats exactly these persisted values as untrusted. The backend slides-tree.ts leg was not supplied, but the text.ts path alone confirms the defect. Minor caveat: the raw modifier interpolation predates this diff, but the claim about the code as written is correct.

findings.finding_key: packages/slides/src/export/pptx/shape.ts::untrusted shape `data.kind` is interpolated into the ooxml `prst` attribute with no allowlist and no escaping — reachable from the v1 content put api that this change now walks

panel.summary: Untrusted shape `data.kind` is interpolated into the OOXML `prst` attribute with no allowlist and no escaping — reachable from the v1 content PUT API that this change now walks
panel.evidence: `kindToPrst(kind)` returns the model value verbatim (`return kind === 'pentagonArrow' ? 'homePlate' : kind;`) and it is interpolated raw at shape.ts:94 `<a:prstGeom prst="${kindToPrst(data.kind)}">`. `ShapeKind` is a type-only union, so the value is whatever JSON was persisted. Attack: PUT /api/v1/workspaces/:wid/documents/:did/content with `{"meta":{...},"themes":[],"masters":[],"layouts":[],"slides":[{"id":"s","layoutId":"l","background":{},"notes":[],"elements":[{"id":"e","type":"shape","frame":{},"data":{"kind":"rect\"/><a:evil x=\""}}]}]}`. The new `assertValidElement` (docs-content.controller.ts:504-556) walks exactly this element and validates only `data.text` block styles, so `data.kind` passes; `writeSlidesRoot` (slides-tree.ts:105) stores `slides` verbatim. Any later PPTX export by a viewer emits attacker-chosen XML into ppt/slides/slideN.xml. This is the same sink class the change hardened for `w:jc`/`algn`/`srgbClr val`, missed here.

fixer.note_prose: NOT CARRIED — see meta.caveats; a fix-agent note quotes the panel's verdict

pass1.reasoning: The diff confirms the enabling premises: the new assertValidElement (docs-content.controller.ts) validates only data.text for shape elements, never data.kind, and the PR states writeSlidesRoot persists slides verbatim. The PR hardens exactly this sink class elsewhere in the same exporter (ALGN/UNDERLINE_STYLE_TO_U Maps, listLevel clamp, srgbClr normalization in packages/slides/src/export/pptx/text.ts and color.ts) but never touches shape.ts, so a raw `prst="${kindToPrst(data.kind)}"` interpolation would be a genuinely missed sink of the same kind. I could not read shape.ts:94 itself (no checkout mounted), so the core code quote is unverified — hence medium confidence — but the claim is internally coherent and every checkable premise holds against the diff.

pass2.reasoning: Verified in packages/slides/src/export/pptx/shape.ts: kindToPrst returns the model string verbatim and shapeToXml interpolates it into `<a:prstGeom prst="${kindToPrst(data.kind)}">` with no allowlist or escaping, while the same function escapes el.id. Verified in packages/backend/src/api/v1/docs-content.controller.ts that assertValidElement checks only id/type/frame and, for shape elements, only data.text — data.kind passes untouched and writeSlidesRoot persists slides verbatim. The chain (PUT hostile kind → stored → PPTX export emits attacker XML) is exactly the sink class the PR hardened for algn/w:jc/srgbClr but missed here. Requires workspace write access and the payload lands in an exported file, so major rather than critical.

panel.summary: `toSrgbHex` now routes theme colors through `toRgbHexColor` with a black fallback — untested, and the existing theme test mirrors the OLD implementation
panel.evidence: packages/slides/test/export/pptx/theme.test.ts only ever calls `themeToXml(defaultLight, 1)`; every color assertion uses well-formed `#RRGGBB` values. Its round-trip test (lines 63-79) recomputes the expected value with `h.replace(/^#/, '').toUpperCase()` — literally the old `toSrgbHex` body — so it passes identically before and after the change and cannot detect a regression in the new normalizer. No test feeds a theme color that `toRgbHexColor` rejects (e.g. `'#FFF"/><a:srgbClr val="000000'`, `'rgb(1,2,3)'`, `''`) to pin either the injection-free `[0-9A-F]{6}` guarantee or the documented `'000000'` degradation.
